value: How can cognitive neuroscience techniques contribute to economic experiments on decision making, and which stages of the decision process can each technique address?

A literature review that maps cognitive-neuroscience measurement techniques (fMRI, EEG, fNIRS, GSR, heart rate, eye-tracking) onto Simon's three phases of the decision-making process and identifies which pairings have and have not yet been exploited in economic experiments.

Cognitive neuroscience is a new and rapidly developing field of multidisciplinary research. It brings together many different scientific domains, chiefly psychology and neurobiology, but also philosophy, linguistics and many other sciences that incorporate the study of the mind in their programs

The commonly used techniques of cognitive neuroscience can be divided into four main groups (Zaleśkiewicz, 2008; Shiv et al., 2005): – neuroimaging of the brain, – neurophysiological techniques, – examination of individual nerve cells, – neuropsychological techniques (the study of neurological patients with brain damage)

Neuroimaging is associated with a group of research methods used to studying the structure and function of the brain. Among them there are electro- and magneto-physiological techniques, exploring the electrical and magnetic activity of neurons, and tomographic methods in which inferences about neuronal activity are made indirectly (Jaśkowski, 2009). Generally, in the area of economic sciences the most applicable methods are: electroencephalography (EEG) and functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI)

EEG is focused on the measurement of brain electrical activity recorded by electrodes placed on the scalp at specific locations (Purves et al., 2013). Because of its very good temporal resolution, this method is usually used to study changes in brain activity in time and to analyse reactions to external stimuli

In such applications, fMRI is much better suited. With its help, you can tell how much oxygen is delivered to specific parts of the brain and deduce their activity. This data contributes to the understanding of the biological basis underlying a performed task

there is another one, quite novel imaging method, i.e. functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) – a non-invasive technique for the optical estimation of cortical activity. It relies on the low optical absorption of the biological tissue of the infrared radiation in the 650–1000 nm wavelength window (Ferrari, Quaresima, 2012). That represents a powerful tool to non-invasively study task-evoked brain activity

Neurophysiological techniques are based on the correlation of brain functions with physiological sensations (Zaleśkiewicz, 2008). The most frequently used (especially in experiments on the effect of emotions on the actions and cognitive functions of respondents) are the measurements of galvanic skin-response (GSR), heart rate (HR) and eye-tracking (ET). The reason for their popularity is relatively simple, in comparison to neuroimaging, registration and the interpretation of signals
The GSR measurement is based on detecting electrical changes in the skin (Dawson, Schell, Filion, 2007) and it is mostly performed on the skin of the hand (fingers)

Eye-tracking, on the other hand, is an effective tool for experimental research because of its abilities to detect the eye position, gaze direction, sequence of eye movement and visual adaptation during cognitive activities. With appropriate software, ET provides both a quantitative and qualitative analysis of the gaze, which is very useful in understanding choice and decision making behaviour

Generally speaking, a decision-making process (simply called a decision process) begins with the awareness of a decision problem, and ends up with a final solution among finite or infinite alternatives. A general decision-making process proposed by Simon (1960, 1977) involves three main phases: Intelligence, Design, and Choice

Intelligence (identification) activity involves gathering and processing information, providing cues for recognizing potential decision needs or opportunities (diagnosis), and for formulating alternatives. Design (development) activity involves identifying alternative courses of action in order to determine likely outcomes and whether these outcomes will satisfy the needs or goals associated with the decision. In the choice (selection) activity, decision-makers make judgements and choose among the previously identified alternatives

Other authors, like Mintzberg, Raisinghani and Theoret (1976), propose slightly different terms to name these stages: Identification, Development and Selection. Despite the differences in naming convention, these three following stages of the decision making process consist of very similar activities

value: Neuroscience techniques can surface fundamental principles of decision making - such as the effect of physical environment, mood or cultural background - that traditional economic research treated as irrelevant.
quote: They may reveal fundamental principles of decision making that may not have been considered relevant in traditional economic research.

value: Every later model of the decision process still contains Simon's three phases of intelligence, design and choice, differing only in naming and in how finely the phases are split.
quote: However, the three main phases proposed by Simon are always present (although sometimes with slightly diff erent names), and all existent models are in many respects similar (Fredrickson, 1985; Gore et al., 1992; Schwenk, 1984).

value: Behavioural experiments can document that people deviate from expected utility theory, but only cognitive neuroscience can supply the explanation of why they are not as rational as the theory assumes.
quote: Experimental economics has an insight into some deviations from the EU theory on the basis of behavioural evidence given by the participants of research but only with cognitive neuroscience would it be possible to find some explanations why people do not behave as rationally as they are supposed to.

value: Both the decision-making and the cognitive neuroscience literatures have concentrated on the final phase of the process - evaluation and choice - leaving the intelligence and design phases comparatively unstudied.
quote: The existing decision-making literature in general, and the cognitive neuroscience literature in particular, has focused especially on the last phase of the decision making process: evaluation and choice (Fellows, 2004) and this aspect has been the most intensively studied to date.

value: The cost of the specialised equipment, fMRI above all, is one of the practical obstacles to using neuroscience in economic experiments.
